import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Editable list: one entry per strategy (family + parameters).
# normal      -> params: mu, sigma
# student_t   -> params: nu, mu, sigma
# skew_normal -> params: xi, omega, alpha
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
STRATEGIES = [
    {'title': 'A1 analytics-game_mgmt: Model-faithful 4th-down and 2-pt aggression',
     'family': 'skew_normal',
     'params': {'xi': 0.30, 'omega': 0.40, 'alpha': 2.0},
     'most_plausible': 0.50},
    {'title': 'A2 analytics-offense: Early-down dropback bias with heavy play-action',
     'family': 'normal',
     'params': {'mu': 0.45, 'sigma': 0.434},
     'most_plausible': 0.45},
    {'title': 'A3 analytics-defense: Two-high light-box coverage-first defense',
     'family': 'normal',
     'params': {'mu': 0.30, 'sigma': 0.383},
     'most_plausible': 0.30},
    {'title': 'I1 intuition-game_mgmt: Proactive timeout spending',
     'family': 'skew_normal',
     'params': {'xi': 0.305, 'omega': 0.382, 'alpha': -2.0},
     'most_plausible': 0.10},
    {'title': 'I2 intuition-offense: Standing chaos package',
     'family': 'student_t',
     'params': {'nu': 4.0, 'mu': 0.20, 'sigma': 0.396},
     'most_plausible': 0.20},
    {'title': 'I3 intuition-defense: Late-rotation disguise with cross-trained DBs',
     'family': 'student_t',
     'params': {'nu': 7.0, 'mu': 0.25, 'sigma': 0.423},
     'most_plausible': 0.25},
]

def build_dist(spec):
    fam = spec['family']
    p = spec['params']
    if fam == 'normal':
        return stats.norm(loc=p['mu'], scale=p['sigma'])
    if fam == 'student_t':
        return stats.t(df=p['nu'], loc=p['mu'], scale=p['sigma'])
    if fam == 'skew_normal':
        return stats.skewnorm(a=p['alpha'], loc=p['xi'], scale=p['omega'])
    raise ValueError('unknown family: ' + fam)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(17, 9))
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, spec in zip(axes, STRATEGIES):
    dist = build_dist(spec)
    lo = float(dist.ppf(0.025))
    hi = float(dist.ppf(0.975))
    span = hi - lo
    xs = np.linspace(lo - 0.35 * span, hi + 0.35 * span, 800)
    ys = dist.pdf(xs)
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color='black', lw=1.5)
    mask = (xs >= lo) & (xs <= hi)
    ax.fill_between(xs[mask], 0.0, ys[mask], color='steelblue', alpha=0.35,
                    label='central 95% via ppf: [' + format(lo, '.2f') + ', ' + format(hi, '.2f') + ']')
    mp = spec['most_plausible']
    ax.axvline(mp, color='crimson', linestyle='--', lw=1.5,
               label='most plausible = ' + format(mp, '.2f'))
    ax.axvline(0.0, color='gray', lw=0.8, linestyle=':')
    ax.set_title(spec['title'], fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel('Change in own scoring margin (points)')
    ax.set_ylabel('density')
    ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc='upper right')
    print(spec['title'])
    print('  family: ' + spec['family'] + ' | params: ' + str(spec['params']))
    print('  ppf-based 95% interval: [' + format(lo, '.3f') + ', ' + format(hi, '.3f') + ']')

fig.suptitle('Subjective priors: per-game scoring-margin effect of each strategy', fontsize=13)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.95))
plt.show()

quantity.description: Change in own-team expected single-game scoring margin from adopting the strategy
quantity.support: unbounded real; positive favors own team

prior.consistency_check: 0.50 lies inside [0.10, 1.20]; skew-normal support is the whole real line, so signed effects are covered. Fitted parameters reproduce ppf interval approx [0.10, 1.19] and mode approx 0.51 - small approximation noted.

distribution_family.justification: Downside is bounded because the policy is reversible and models rarely endorse clearly bad gos, while the upside versus a passive baseline is larger; that asymmetry calls for a right-skewed family.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Chose alpha=+2 for moderate right skew. Standard SN(0,1,2) has approx q025=-0.509, q975=+2.237, mode=+0.533 (numeric). omega=(1.20-0.10)/(2.237+0.509)=1.10/2.746=0.40; xi=0.10+0.509*0.40=0.30. Implied mode=0.30+0.533*0.40=0.51 vs stated 0.50; fit numerically, ~0.01-pt approximation.

strategies.rationale: Public EPA/WP models (Romer-style analysis, nfl4th-type bots) consistently show punts and short field goals in these spots burn win probability; even after the league-wide shift, typical teams still leave roughly 0.2-0.5 wins per season here. That converts to a few tenths of a point of margin per game at essentially zero implementation cost.
strategies.recommendation: Pre-commit to a win-probability-model policy: go for it on most 4th-and-1/2 beyond our own 30, treat the opponent 35-55 as four-down territory, and follow the two-point chart (e.g., go for 2 when down 8, down 2, or up 1 late). Decisions are scripted Friday, not improvised Sunday.
strategies.title: Model-faithful fourth-down and two-point aggression

prior.consistency_check: 0.45 lies inside [-0.40, 1.30]; normal support is the whole real line. mu +/- 1.96*sigma = [-0.40, 1.30], matching the stated interval.

distribution_family.justification: This is a well-studied lever where equilibrium adaptation by defenses and execution risk (sacks, turnovers) roughly mirror the upside, so a symmetric, moderate-tailed family fits.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Public play-by-play work shows early-down passes out-earn runs by roughly 0.1 EPA per play and that play-action efficiency does not require an established run game; reallocating 5-7 snaps per game is worth around half a point of margin before defenses adapt. Most teams remain more run-heavy on early downs than the models justify.
strategies.recommendation: In neutral game states, raise 1st/2nd-down dropback rate to roughly 58-62% with a play-action share near a third of dropbacks, saving called runs for light boxes and obvious leverage situations.
strategies.title: Early-down dropback bias with heavy play-action

prior.consistency_check: 0.30 lies inside [-0.45, 1.05]; normal support is the whole real line. mu +/- 1.96*sigma = [-0.451, 1.051], matching the stated interval to rounding.

distribution_family.justification: Gains from suppressing explosive passes and losses against heavy rushing teams feel roughly mirror-image, and the league trend toward two-high shrinks the residual edge; symmetric with moderate tails.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Pass defense, not run defense, predicts points allowed; conceding 4-yard runs to prevent explosive passes is an EPA-positive trade, and public charting shows blitzes lose more in coverage than they gain in pressure on average. Many teams still over-invest in stopping the league's least efficient play type.
strategies.recommendation: Make split-safety shells with 6-man boxes the base call on early downs, rush four, blitz below league average, and shift roster and practice resources from run-stuffing to coverage depth.
strategies.title: Two-high, light-box, coverage-first defense

prior.consistency_check: 0.10 lies inside [-0.55, 0.50]; skew-normal support is the whole real line. Fitted parameters give ppf interval approx [-0.55, 0.49] and mode approx 0.10 - honest near-zero center with wide interval reflects a deliberately weak claim.

distribution_family.justification: The upside is small and capped (a timeout can only rescue so much), but the failure mode - needing a hoarded timeout late and not having it - is rare and costly, giving a longer left tail.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

strategies.rationale: Why intuition: public analytics prices timeouts well in end-game models but is essentially silent on the early-game value of avoiding one wasted high-leverage snap, and convention says hoard. My judgment is that saving a conversion attempt (a 2-4 expected-point swing) usually beats the option value of a third late timeout, while the rare game where the missing timeout matters creates real downside.
strategies.recommendation: Treat the first two timeouts of each half as insurance on high-leverage snaps: burn one to escape a busted call, wrong personnel, or imminent delay penalty on 3rd/4th-and-short or in the red zone, rather than hoarding all three for a two-minute drill that often never materializes.
strategies.title: Proactive timeout spending as play-quality insurance

prior.consistency_check: 0.20 lies inside [-0.90, 1.30]; Student-t support is the whole real line. mu +/- 2.776*sigma = [-0.899, 1.299], matching the stated interval.

distribution_family.justification: With almost no usable public data, there is a non-trivial chance the true effect is surprisingly large in either direction (explosive gains vs turnovers and short fields), so a heavy-tailed symmetric family is honest.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu=4 for clearly heavy tails; t critical value t_{0.975,4} = 2.776. mu = most_plausible = 0.20. sigma = (1.30 - (-0.90)) / (2 * 2.776) = 2.20 / 5.552 = 0.396 (scale, not SD).

strategies.rationale: Why intuition: public trick-play samples are tiny and selection-biased, and the mechanism I actually believe in - taxing the opponent's limited practice week and forcing simplified defensive calls that help my base offense - is invisible in public data. My judgment is the prep tax plus occasional explosive beats the turnover and negative-play risk, but the true effect could plausibly be near zero and the tails are fat in both directions.
strategies.recommendation: Carry a permanent menu of 8-10 deeply rehearsed unconventional calls (double passes, throwback screens, unbalanced and swinging-gate alignments, sudden tempo bursts after explosive plays) and script 2-3 into every first half regardless of opponent.
strategies.title: Standing chaos package: rehearsed gadget and tempo cluster

prior.consistency_check: 0.25 lies inside [-0.75, 1.25]; Student-t support is the whole real line. mu +/- 2.365*sigma = [-0.750, 1.250], matching the stated interval.

distribution_family.justification: Opponent- and QB-dependent payoffs plus bust risk produce outliers in both directions, but coaching reps temper the extremes; nu=7 gives moderately heavy symmetric tails.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu=7 for moderately heavy tails; t critical value t_{0.975,7} = 2.365. mu = most_plausible = 0.25. sigma = (1.25 - (-0.75)) / (2 * 2.365) = 2.00 / 4.730 = 0.423 (scale, not SD).

strategies.rationale: Why intuition: the value of disguise is essentially unmeasured publicly - tracking-data research is nascent and mixed, and bust rates and practice costs are private - so this rests on my read that breaking a QB's pre-snap rules slows processing and manufactures sacks and turnovers, with the biggest payoff against elite rhythm passers. Blown rotations and degraded run fits create genuine downside, so the floor is real.
strategies.recommendation: Cross-train safeties and nickels so nearly every snap shows the same two-high pre-snap picture, then rotate into the actual coverage at or after the snap on a majority of dropbacks, deliberately decoupling the shell shown from the coverage family played. This is about concealment, not structure - it layers on top of whatever base defense we run.
strategies.title: Late-rotation coverage disguise with cross-trained DBs
